qs.q: Which of the following defines compound heterozygotes classified under sickle cell disease?
o: Both beta-globin alleles carry the sickle cell mutation and an alpha-thalassemia gene
One beta-globin allele has the sickle cell mutation and the second has a mutation such as HbC or beta-thalassemia
Both beta-globin alleles carry mutations other than the sickle cell mutation like HbOArab and HbD
One beta-globin allele has normal hemoglobin while both alpha-globin alleles carry HbS
qs.e: Sickle cell disease includes compound heterozygotes where one beta-globin allele has the sickle cell mutation and the second allele includes a mutation such as HbC, beta-thalassemia, HbD, or HbOArab. Homozygous HbSS occurs when both beta-globin alleles carry the sickle cell mutation.

qs.q: What is the most common clinical manifestation and the most distinguishing clinical feature of sickle cell disease?
o: Aplastic crisis presenting with sudden drop in hemoglobin levels and reticulocytopenia
Acute chest syndrome presenting with chest pain, fever, and new pulmonary infiltrates
Hand-foot syndrome presenting with painful swelling of the hands and feet in infants
Vaso-occlusive pain crisis presenting with acute and chronic pain episodes
qs.e: Vaso-occlusive crisis presenting with acute and chronic pain is the most common clinical manifestation and distinguishing feature of sickle cell disease. Other complications like aplastic crisis or acute chest syndrome are serious but less frequent as baseline features.

qs.q: A child with sickle cell disease presents with fever, severe anemia, and reticulocytopenia. Which underlying infection should be presumed?
o: Streptococcus pneumoniae infection leading to invasive bacterial pneumonia
Human parvovirus B19 infection leading to transient red cell aplasia
Salmonella species infection leading to osteomyelitis and bacteremia
Haemophilus influenzae type b infection leading to acute epiglottitis
qs.e: Any child with sickle cell disease, fever, and reticulocytopenia should be presumed to have a parvovirus B19 infection causing an aplastic crisis. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Salmonella are common bacterial pathogens causing different clinical presentations.

qs.q: Which imaging modality is specifically used to identify children with sickle cell disease who are at high risk for a stroke?
o: Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography
Chest radiography examination
Abdominal ultrasonography study
Technetium-99m bone scanning
qs.e: Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography can identify children with sickle cell disease at high risk for stroke. Chest radiography is used for respiratory symptoms, and abdominal ultrasound evaluates organ sizes and biliary disease.

qs.q: Which bacterial organisms pose the greatest danger for severe infection in adult patients with sickle cell disease?
o: Gram-positive encapsulated organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae
Gram-negative organisms, especially Salmonella species and agents
Atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae respiratory strains
Anaerobic organisms such as Bacteroides fragilis and related flora
qs.e: While children are primarily vulnerable to encapsulated organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae, adult infections in sickle cell disease are predominantly with gram-negative organisms, especially Salmonella. Staphylococcus aureus is also associated with osteomyelitis evaluations.

qs.q: Which clinical finding characterizes hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) in young children with sickle cell disease?
o: Bilateral painful and swollen hands and/or feet in young children
Painless ulceration of the lower extremities in older patients
Rapid enlargement of the spleen with left upper quadrant pain
Upper lobe pulmonary infiltrates with fever and tachypnea
qs.e: Hand-foot syndrome is a dactylitis presenting as bilateral painful and swollen hands and/or feet in children. Leg ulcers present as chronic painful problems in older patients, unlike the acute dactylitis seen in infancy and early childhood.

qs.q: Which diagnostic study should be considered in a febrile child with sickle cell disease who appears toxic or exhibits neurologic findings such as neck stiffness?
o: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain for structural evaluation
Cerebrospinal fluid examination via lumbar puncture procedure
Transcranial near-infrared spectroscopy for oxygenation monitoring
Pulmonary function testing to assess respiratory capacity
qs.e: CSF examination via lumbar puncture should be considered in febrile children who appear toxic and in those with neurologic findings like neck stiffness or positive Brudzinski/Kernig signs. CT scanning may be considered before the LP if focal deficits or increased pressure are suspected.

qs.q: What is the most distinguishing clinical feature and common manifestation of sickle cell disease?
o: An aplastic crisis
A vaso-occlusive pain crisis
An acute splenic sequestration
A hand-foot syndrome presentation
qs.e: Vaso-occlusive crisis and pain crises are the most distinguishing clinical feature of sickle cell disease. Aplastic crisis and splenic sequestration are serious complications rather than the most common distinguishing feature.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sickle cell disease is an inherited hemoglobin disorder causing rigid, sickle‑shaped red cells that lead to vaso‑occlusion, hemolytic anemia, and organ damage. Diagnosis relies on hemoglobin electrophoresis and peripheral smear; management focuses on preventing crises and infection.

sections.p: Sickle cell disease comprises a group of autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathies, most commonly HbSS, where a β‑globin mutation (Glu6Val) produces HbS. Under low oxygen, HbS polymerizes, distorting red cells.
b: Diagnostic criteria: HbS ≥ 50% on electrophoresis or HPLC, plus clinical features.
Peripheral smear shows sickle‑shaped RBCs, target cells, and Howell‑Jolly bodies.

t.b: Confirms type and proportion of HbS vs HbF/HbA; >90% HbS in homozygous disease.
Identifies sickle cells and degree of hemolysis; guides urgency of care.
Detects disease before symptoms; enables early prophylaxis.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by frequency of vaso‑occlusive crises, organ involvement, and laboratory markers (e.g., hemoglobin, LDH). The Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease Severity Score (PSCDSS) and adult complications index are used.
b: Mild: ≤2 crises/year, no organ damage.
Moderate: 3‑5 crises/year or early organ changes (e.g., splenomegaly).
Severe: >5 crises/year, stroke, pulmonary hypertension, or renal failure.

sections.p: The primary cause is the β‑globin point mutation (HbS). Co‑existing factors that worsen sickling are common in low‑resource settings.
b: HbSS genotype (most common cause).
Co‑inherited α‑thalassemia can modify severity.
Infections (malaria, bacterial sepsis, HIV) increase sickling risk.
Dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis, and extreme temperatures trigger crises.

sections.p: Patients present with chronic hemolytic anemia and acute vaso‑occlusive events. In infants, dactylitis is typical; older children and adults develop pain crises, splenic sequestration, and organ dysfunction.
b: Painful swelling of hands/feet (dactylitis) in <2 y.
Recurrent bone pain crises, often in long bones.
Anemia‑related fatigue, jaundice, gallstones.
Functional asplenia → fever = emergency.

sections.p: Beyond confirming diagnosis, labs assess hemolysis, organ function, and infection risk.
b: CBC with reticulocyte count evaluates anemia severity.
LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin track hemolysis.
Renal and liver panels monitor end‑organ damage.

t.b: Quantifies anemia and reticulocytosis; low Hb with high retic suggests hemolysis.
Screens for elevated cerebral blood flow velocity; predicts stroke risk.
Detects acute chest syndrome; infiltrates require urgent care.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require rapid intervention.
b: Acute chest syndrome: fever, chest pain, hypoxia.
Stroke: focal neurologic deficit, seizures.
Splenic sequestration: sudden abdominal fullness, drop in Hb.
Severe infection (especially encapsulated bacteria).

sections.p: Treatment combines disease‑modifying therapy, crisis prevention, and supportive care.
b: Hydroxyurea increases HbF, reducing crises; first‑line disease‑modifying drug.
Penicillin prophylaxis (until age 5) prevents pneumococcal sepsis.
Vaccinations: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, influenza.
Acute pain: IV opioids, hydration, oxygen if hypoxic.
Blood transfusion for severe anemia, stroke prevention, or ACS.

sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents complications and guides therapy adjustments.
b: Quarterly clinic visits with CBC, HbF level, and growth assessment.
Annual transcranial Doppler in children 2‑16 y.
Education on hydration, temperature avoidance, and early fever reporting.
Thalassemia major – also causes severe anemia but lacks sickle cells.
G6PD deficiency – hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress, not vaso‑occlusion.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia – positive Coombs test, no sickling.
Fetal hemoglobin may be high in early infancy, masking sickling on smear.
Normal peripheral smear in early disease if sample taken during a transfusion.
Low HbF after hydroxyurea non‑adherence can be misinterpreted as disease progression.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C in any child with SCD (risk of sepsis).
Chest pain, shortness of breath, or new infiltrate on X‑ray (acute chest syndrome).
Sudden severe abdominal pain with rapid Hb drop (splenic sequestration).

faq.q: Why do patients with SCD become functionally asplenic?
faq.a: Repeated splenic infarction from sickling destroys splenic tissue, eliminating its ability to clear encapsulated bacteria.
It increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which inhibits HbS polymerization, reducing sickling and pain crises.

faq.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated?
faq.a: For severe anemia, acute chest syndrome, stroke prevention, or splenic sequestration with rapid Hb decline.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of vaso‑occlusive crises and how hydroxyurea modifies it.
List the acute complications of sickle cell disease that require immediate hospitalization.
Interpret a hemoglobin electrophoresis report showing 90% HbS, 5% HbF, and 5% HbA2.
